title: When Multiple People Are Accountable to the Same Problem or Outcome
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post argues that holding several people accountable for the same outcome backfires. Leaders assume more owners raise the odds of success, but diffusion of responsibility means nobody truly owns the result. The author insists that accountability is individual, so a team's outcome belongs to the team leader or co-leaders. He notes that leaders often assign shared accountability by accident, simply by not naming one person when describing a goal. The move is to reframe accountability as a solitary act while leaving many people responsible for the actions that lead to the result. The closing image is that spreading accountability means holding many feet to a fire that never lights.
points: Multiple parties cannot be accountable for an outcome, only individuals can.
Spreading responsibility lets people hide in the group and give only partial oversight.
Leaders often create shared accountability unknowingly by failing to name a specific owner.
Many can be responsible for actions, but only one person answers for the outcome.
quotes: Unfortunately, instead of ensuring success, this tactic actually reduces the odds of a favorable outcome. When multiple parties are accountable, then no one truly is. Multiple parties can never be truly accountable. Only individuals can.

By spreading responsibility to multiple people, leaders guarantee no one will feel or act like they own the problem or outcome. In numbers, people find the camouflage and cover to duck full responsibility.

Asking a team to be accountable is a common mistake that frequently undermines performance and produces mediocre outcomes. By insisting that a team or group be accountable, no one takes control and owns the end result. Everyone on the team presumes someone else will drive the bus.
Any time a leader doesn’t specify a particular leader or team member to be accountable to the desired outcome, the presumption is that everyone is being held to that standard.
Accountability is a solitary act. That doesn’t mean multiple parties are not responsible for the actions that lead to the result. But only one person can answer for the outcome.
